articles.description:
I wrote something down recently, and later I couldn't find it. If you know me, you know why; I put my notes into too many different apps.
Once in a while I declare loudly that "I'm using only this app, from now on! I mean it!" and then change my mind a month later. It's just the way I am. This most recent failure was the last straw and finally forced me to deal with it properly.
Instead of fixing myself, I built a software crutch. I spent today vibe-coding an indexer and search engine for all of my stuff. Here's the initial version of a web UI:

I also hacked together a TUI and an Emacs package. Those access the data via Tailscale SSH so I don't need to worry about installing things on other machines. Just the wrapper script.
Here's the list of sources being indexed (so far):
./archive index
baty.net: 1272 items (0.9s)
archive.baty.net: 2791 items (1.1s)
linux.baty.net: 26 items (0.0s)
blot.baty.net: 678 items (0.3s)
jackbaty.com: 581 items (0.1s)
notes: 2287 items (1.0s)
dayone: 2507 items (1.4s)
thebrain: 1177 items (0.5s)
mail: 1 updated, 0 removed (since revision 43773) (1.6s)
duplicates: 786 items in 381 groups (10.2s)

One nice thing about this is now I can search all of my Denote notes from my phone.
Everything is plain files and it uses boring, durable tools, so the archive should outlive whichever apps made the content that week. Even an AI layer, if I add one, sits on top of the search instead of being built into it. The database is disposable because it only takes 10 seconds to reindex everything.
Maybe now I'll be OK with all of my app churn.
✍️ Reply by email
articles.title: A searchable archive of everything

articles.description:
has an interesting problem whose solution is harder than you think it would be. The problem is pretty simple: Every Sunday morning when he writes his weekly review, he needs to update all the clock tables in his journal. That usually takes about a minute and mbork had the idea that he could use an idle timer to run the update. Specifically, he reasoned that if Emacs were idle for a minute it probably meant that he was otherwise engaged and that Emacs would be idle for another minute so why not fire off his update?


Of course, he wanted to do this only once a week on Sundays so it was a bit more complex than just setting the idle timer. He came up with the idea of setting a (normal) timer for 3 AM on Sunday that would set the idle timer. That didn’t quite work because of a technical issue but he got things working with yet another timer.


You should read his post for the details. His solution is interesting and shows that sometimes even simple things can be harder than we imagined.
articles.title: Irreal: Updating Clock Tables

articles.description:
techhub.social, lispwizard has a short post (or whatever techhub.social calls them) on saving window configurations to registers. He notes how easy it is to save multiple configurations and switch between them on the fly.


Saving window configurations and other data in registers is an extraordinarily powerful technique that all Emacs users should learn and master. There’s a problem, though, when you want to do this programmatically: which register should you use? How can you be sure that your choice won’t conflict with a register that the user has chosen manually for some other task? There are several situations in which I want to run an Emacs function in a single window—Elfeed is an example—and I do that by saving the current window configuration, deleting the other windows, running the required function, and then restoring the previous window configuration but how do I choose a “safe” register to save the window configuration in?


The answer is a trick I learned from Magnar Sveen years ago. Instead of using a letter to name the register, you use a symbol like :saved-windows. That works because when you name a register with a letter, Emacs uses a pointer to its symbol as the register name. Using a symbol name like :saved-windows works because the result is also a symbol pointer.


If you have the need to save something in a register programmatically, this is a good way of doing it. You don’t have to worry about conflicts  because the user can not use symbol names for registers interactively.
articles.title: Irreal: Saving Window Configurations

a simple package that trades Org mode’s heading stars for UTF-8 bullets. If you’re like me, your first thought is, “Doesn’t that already exist?” Sort of. What already exists is the no longer maintained org-bullets. Cherti’s package is called org-ibullets (note the i).


Cherti explains the differences from org-bullets in his announcement. The TL;DR is that he’s optimized org-ibullets by eliminating redundant computations, eliminated spurious syntax warnings that org-bullets could produce, and made some improvements at the source level.


As I said, the package is simple. It can be used right out of the box but you can customize the list of bullets and their face if you desire. This seems like a very nice package if you’d like to make your Org buffers look a little nicer.

1. I did have this post from Curtis McHale about the future of Emacs interaction in my TODO queue so I decided to do a quick write up about it.


McHale’s contention is that we use keyboards because they’re the best way of interfacing with computers. He points to everybody’s favorite keyboard replacement, voice input, but notes that even on Star Trek—that arguably popularized the idea—Captain Picard still tells his crew members where he wants to go and they type in the commands at their control stations.


As I said in my last post on the matter. my written thoughts are always much better organized than my verbal ones so moving to spoken input would be a net loss for me. Still, it will be interesting to see how things play out.

1 



OK, OK. Maybe that overstates my usual efforts. I blame whatever sickness I have for that.

articles.description:
For more than a decade the Clojure REPL most people saw in a terminal was
REPLy, the one behind lein repl. It
served us well, but it’s showing its age, and I kept wishing for a terminal
REPL that felt like CIDER, without the Emacs part. So I finally built one.
neorepl 0.1 is out today!
Why another REPL?
There’s no shortage of Clojure REPLs, so it’s fair to ask. Here’s what I was
after:
nREPL all the way down. neorepl only speaks nREPL, so it works with anything
that runs an nREPL server: Clojure, babashka, shadow-cljs, Basilisp,
ClojureCLR and so on. The smarts live on the server. When cider-nrepl is
there neorepl uses it, the same way CIDER does, and when it isn’t it falls
back to nREPL’s built-in ops, and then to evaluating a bit of code.
A REPL that’s pleasant to use: a proper line edit…

articles.description:
quick post on Sacha’s solution to a problem posed by David Pape. I thought it was a nice solution but then 0-_-0_ pointed out that abo-abo had already solved this problem with his tiny library. So I wrote about that and prepared to move on.


I was not allowed to. Frequent commenter Phil remarked in my original post that he would use a keyboard macro. He suggested that that would make sense for those of us who who seldom need to enter a sequence of ranges like Pape. In Pape’s case this was something that he needed to do a lot so a solution like Sacha’s or abo-abo’s make sense. I agree with Phil. A keyboard macro is exactly how I would solve this problem given that I seldom have it.


This seems pretty obvious and might not be worth writing about except that Phil’s solution showed me something that I didn’t know: You can set the initial value of the counter with a Ctrl+u n where n is the desired initial value. That’s a lot easier than using Ctrl+x Ctrl+k Ctrl+c to do the job.


As a final note, I think that Phil had a typo in his macro. As far as I can tell it should be

C-u 47 <f3> # <f3> , SPC <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4>


At least that’s what works for me.


It turns out that I regularly use a macro with a counter so I’m really happy to learn that the counter can be set so easily.


Update [2026-10-10 Sat 12:12]: Fixed link.
articles.title: Irreal: Still More On Entering Ranges

articles.description:
on Sacha Chua’s solution for entering number ranges, 0-_-0_ points out that a solution already exists. That solution is abo-abo’s tiny library. I vaguely remember seeing tiny when abo-abo released it 13 years ago but I never followed up and used it. Still, anything from abo-abo is worth taking a look at and, in any event, we now have two solutions to the problem.


Abo-abo’s solution brings to mind another Emacs lesson: very often, if you need some functionality, there’s a good chance that it already exists. Of course, that’s not the same as being easily discoverable. An internal function can usually be discovered through the on-line documentation but a third party library like tiny won’t appear in that documentation until it’s loaded.


That’s it for today. I just wanted to tell the rest of the story from yesterday.
articles.title: Irreal: More On Number Ranges

It was clear that the relationship between Real Madrid and La Liga president Javier Tebas was heading toward disaster when the two parties started bickering in the press less than a month ago, but we've now reached the stage where one is earnestly comparing the behavior of the other to an infamous Nazi.
After Jose Mourinho printed out images of perceived missed calls from the Madrid derby, Tebas blasted Real Madrid for what he felt was a bit of image manipulation, calling the club out for believing itself to be bigger than La Liga itself, all while utilizing the press to drive forward its messaging. In response, Madrid called out what it felt was Tebas's fixation on belittling the winningest club in Spanish soccer history. As I said in September, I thought cooler heads would prevail after how embarrassing that whole situation was for both sides. Boy howdy, was I wrong!
As is proving to be his custom, Tebas woke up on Friday and decided to send yet another ballista bolt at Real Madrid. Specifically, and repeatedly, Tebas attacked the media surrounding the club for what he believes are biased articles and debate segments on Real Madrid TV. His targets this time were Tomás González-Martín and Jesús Urdiola, journalists with El Debate, the same Spanish publication he attacked last time. Tebas raised two specific articles as issues: One, by González-Martín, details Real Madrid's continued fight with the league over the Negreira referee scandal; the other, by Urdiola, is about how Real Madrid feels personally attacked by La Liga's schedule-making.
articles.title: La Liga President Says Real Madrid Is Moving Like Joseph Goebbels

articles.author: Israel Daramola
articles.description:
ESPN is reporting that ESPN and the College Football Playoff are close to a deal to expand the playoff field to 24 teams in 2027. This news arrives merely two years after the field already expanded from four teams to 12. Not only was this expansion inevitable, but it is unlikely to be the last we see.
For now, we are on the cusp of a 24-team playoff, which comes as ESPN and the CFP have been negotiating a big new deal for the network to continue broadcasting the games. According to ESPN's reporting, this new deal will do away with Power 4 conference championship games and start the season a week earlier. Details are reportedly being finalized, but ESPN describes the current composition for the 24-team field as 19 at-large bids, the Power 4 conference champions "as determined by each league," and the highest-ranked Group of 6 team.
The Big Ten has been a leading proponent for this change, and its commissioner Tony Pettiti pushed back against complaints that further expansion would dilute and devalue the product and the games. He argues that the new system would include "tiered incentives." According to ESPN, seeds 1 through 8 would get a first-round bye, followed by a home game. Teams seeded from 9 through 16 would get a first-round home game, while teams seeded 17 and lower should be vying for a higher ranking, both to stay in competition and to get that first-round home game. Cool.
articles.title: The CFP Is Expanding For The Same Reason The PCSA Is Gaining Momentum

Ray: It's been a tough year for Texas A&M and head coach Mike Elko, who celebrated the Aggies' 27-6 loss to Missouri last Saturday by calling the team's leading social media outlet a "cesspool" and, two days later, apologized for calling the team's leading social media outlet a "cesspool." Elko also said that he is the reason Texas A&M is struggling, which is probably what the team's leading social media outlet was saying about him after his team lost at home by three scores. This is that rare case where someone can be right all three times, making Saturday's showdown with The Citadel a must-watch game, just to see what Elko says afterward if his Aggies don't cover the 45.5-point spread. Otherwise, it's just another weekend in college football's version of paradise, if that's what you consider your afterlife goal.
Israel: We are near midseason, and exactly as we predicted the most exciting programs in the sport are Will Stein's Kentucky and Bob Chesney's UCLA. Bill Belichick's UNC team keeps losing, but they're too scrappy and full of energy to make fun of or even care about. Deion Sanders's Colorado team is a complete mess but are too dull and incompetent to fuel much schadenfreude. Lane Kiffin cannot get the stank of the Brian Kelly era off LSU in one offseason, it turns out. And so ends the Los Angeles Dodgers' reign as baseball's most overwhelming boogeyman. The poster kids for the omnipotence of money, the belief that having the best player means being the best team, the power of the big market over all it surveys—all of that feels less important at this moment than the ability to do the things the Milwaukee Brewers do better than anyone else. The same old song has been replaced, for the moment, by this:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7Xzmeye6MaY


Yes, meet your new overlords. The Brewers pack extraordinary amounts of baseball into every game, play it better than anyone else, and supposedly have no interest in hitting home runs. It was fitting, then, that they gave the nation a little tweak on the cheek Thursday night en route to sweeping the Dodgers out of the postseason when the final run they scored in their 6-4 win came on a moonshot from noted Boston Red Sox ex-pat and devoted homer avoider David Hamilton. The Brewers did all the things that made them the best team in baseball this season, and mostly kept the Dodgers from doing the things that won them the last two World Series—and then they did the stuff that contemporary winning baseball teams do, too, in a typically unpredictable way.

I had been going to Dodger Stadium with my dad for about 30 years before he pointed them out to me. “See that?” he asked, gesturing toward two rectangular panels of concrete on a far wall of the main seating structure. They looked almost like friezes, carved with inscrutable designs. My dad had been wondering about them for decades.
Turns out the pieces he’d spotted are just the beginning. Eventually I’d locate more custom bas-relief sculptures around the park—about a dozen in total. Smaller ones visible from the field-level entrances. Massive, multi-story pieces that wrap around certain outside corners of the building. They’re subtle: abstract scenes unadorned with color, camouflaged into the rest of their concrete environments, in some cases obscured by trees and bushes.
articles.title: The Secret History Of Dodger Stadium’s Mysterious Concrete Murals

articles.description:
After a flyout and a strikeout in his first two attempts, Jake Bauers's third time facing Blake Snell in Wednesday's Game 3 of the National League Championship Series went like this: Bauers took a slider down the middle of the plate for strike one. He took two non-competitive pitches down low to make the count 2-1. He foul-tipped a changeup, and then, sitting on two strikes, four pitches into his at-bat, he decided that he simply would not strike out again.
So Bauers fouled off a slider in the zone, then a curveball. He laid off an inside fastball to draw the count full. Then he managed to foul off a high fastball, and, immediately after, slowed down to catch a changeup in the zone. As the pitch count for this at-bat ticked over into double digits, Bauers pulled a slider that sat up in the zone a bit too much, sending it into the stands past the right-field foul pole. On the 11th pitch, Bauers made no mistake. Snell threw a middle-middle, 98-mph fastball, and Bauers smoked a no-doubt, two-run homer that carried over 400 feet into right field to give the Milwaukee Brewers a 3-2 lead.
When Bauers's teammate Garrett Mitchell hit his own home run off Snell just two pitches later, it was, comparatively, an anticlimax. Spiritually speaking, a guy hitting a home run one pitch after just missing out on another home run counts for two home runs. Bauers had already won the game; Mitchell's own homer was just overkill on Snell's way out.
articles.title: It’s Jake Bauerses All The Way Down

I am not a rock star, although I like to imagine myself as one. I imagine it so, so hard: packed stadiums, crowds numbering five figures going wild as I take my shirt off, shady managers hanging out backstage ready to ply me with Hefty bags full of pharmaceutical cocaine. But it’s too late for me, on the cusp of 50, to actually become a rock star — it certainly couldn’t be a skill or charisma issue, no sir — which is why there’s a tiny slice of the hospitality industry that exists to make patrons like me FEEL like rock stars, if only for a brief moment. 

This is where the legendary Phoenix Hotel, plopped down on Eddy Street right in the middle of San Francisco’s Tenderloin neighborhood, comes in.

I have stayed at many hotels in San Francisco, but all of them were hotel hotels. Elevator b…
articles.title: San Francisco's best hotel cannot be killed

There’s a midterm election coming on Nov. 3, which includes a race here in California to determine who will replace Gov. Gavin Newsom. On the blue side of the ticket is unremarkable Democrat Xavier Becerra, whose chief positive attribute is that he is not a Republican. On the red side is Steve Hilton, an immigrant from the U.K. who gained U.S. citizenship in 2021. Hilton’s most high-profile political experience came back in the early 2010s, when he served as an adviser to then-U.K. prime minister and alleged porcine enthusiast David Cameron. But that experience, plus a lengthy stint as a commentator for Fox News, was enough to convince Hilton that he not only should run for governor, but that he WILL be the state’s next governor.

articles.description:
We recently moved from a rural suburb in Massachusetts to a small coastal village in Rhode Island.
It’s been transformative, and I wish I’d done it sooner!
Trickle-Down Effects Unlike a city, a village has homes with yards. Unlike a suburb, a village has businesses and parks intermixed with homes. It’s the best of both worlds.
Being able to walk or bike places has trickle-down effects.
 Instead of driving 20 minutes one-way to get groceries, I can ride my bike there in 5 minutes.
articles.title: Life on Foot

articles.description:
About 14 years ago, we moved out into the rural suburbs. I loved the quiet, the abundant wildlife, and our proximity to farms.
I didn’t realize just how often doing anything at all would require a car.
The Sprawl Absolutely nothing was walkable. We lived at the very top of a very high hill, so things weren’t really bikeable either.
Groceries, restaurants, entertainment, friends, the library, and so on… you need to get in a car and drive at least 15 minutes for all of it.
articles.title: The Village

articles.description:
